title: Humility, Lost Sheep, and Forgiveness
overview: Jesus teaches his followers how to live together: humbly, protecting the vulnerable, going after those who stray, handling wrongs carefully, and forgiving without keeping count.

parts.label: Who is the greatest? (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: The disciples wanted to know who would rank highest, so Jesus put a child in front of them, someone with no status in that world. Real greatness means letting go of the hunt for position, and welcoming such overlooked people is like welcoming Jesus himself.

parts.label: Warnings about stumbling (vv. 6-9)
parts.note: To make someone stumble means to lead them away from faith, and a millstone was a huge grinding stone, so drowning with one would be a better fate. Cutting off a hand or tearing out an eye is understood by most readers as deliberate exaggeration, meaning: deal ruthlessly with whatever pulls you into wrong.

parts.label: The one straying sheep (vv. 10-14)
parts.note: The line about the little ones' angels seeing God's face suggests the vulnerable have God's close attention, though its exact meaning is debated. A shepherd who leaves the flock to find one lost sheep shows that God does not write off anyone who wanders.

parts.label: When someone wrongs you (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: Jesus gives steps aimed at winning the person back: talk privately, then bring one or two witnesses, then tell the community, and only then treat them as an outsider, like the foreigners and distrusted tax collectors of the day. Binding and loosing were Jewish teaching terms for forbidding and allowing, here applied to the group's decisions, and Jesus promises to be present even where two or three meet in his name.

parts.label: How often to forgive? (vv. 21-22)
parts.note: Peter's offer of seven times already seemed generous. Jesus answers seventy seven times (the wording can also mean seventy times seven), which means stop counting altogether.

parts.label: The unforgiving servant (vv. 23-35)
parts.note: A servant is let off a debt of ten thousand of the largest money unit of the day, a fortune no worker could ever repay, then chokes a fellow servant over roughly a hundred days' wages. The ending is harsh: the king hands him over to be tortured, and Jesus says God will treat those who refuse to forgive from the heart in the same way.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the parable's ending means God's forgiveness can actually be withdrawn from someone who will not forgive, or is a vivid warning that truly receiving forgiveness always changes how a person treats others.
think: Do you think there is a point where someone should stop being forgiven, and if so, what would put them past it?
